questions.question: In FeNiCrCoCu/Cu systems at 900 K, does surface damage-induced defect accumulation (hypothesis) or Cu melting (mechanism principle) primarily drive the sharp wear resistance drop, and how can TEM dislocation counts and HCP fraction be measured to distinguish them?
questions.rationale: The paper proposes two competing mechanisms (surface defects hindering dislocations vs. Cu matrix melting) for the sharp drop in wear resistance at 900 K. Determining the dominant mechanism is critical for selecting the correct mitigation strategy (e.g., surface hardening vs. melting point modification).
questions.decision_use: Selects between surface engineering approaches to suppress defect accumulation versus thermal stabilization strategies to prevent Cu melting.
answer_requirements: Post-friction TEM imaging to quantify dislocation line length and density at the interface
Atom probe tomography or diffraction to measure local Cu liquid fraction and HCP atom fraction at 900 K
Correlation analysis between HCP fraction increase and wear volume loss
evidence_spans: This might be due to a large number of surface defects in the Cu matrix under the high temperature environment, which hindered the generation of line defect dislocation.
This might be due to the damage of the contact surface caused by the penetration of the coating into the matrix under the pressure of the indenter at high temperature.
This was because the temperature was close to the melting point of the Cu matrix material, resulting in a significant decrease in the hardness of the material
During the friction process, a large number of disordered structures appeared and began to melt, and the stacking faults also began to decrease at 1200 K.
When the temperature reaches 900 K, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating decreases sharply

questions.question: Does introducing surface roughness to the FeNiCrCoCu coating (a rejected alternative) alter the friction coefficient fluctuation trend observed between 900 K and 1200 K, and how can this be tested via variable roughness nanoindentation?
questions.rationale: The authors explicitly rejected studying roughness. However, given the intense fluctuation of friction coefficients at high temperatures and the role of surface defects, roughness might be a critical variable to control or exploit for wear stabilization.
questions.decision_use: Decides whether to invest in surface roughness control processes as a critical step for high-temperature wear stability.
answer_requirements: Perform nanoindentation on FeNiCrCoCu coatings with systematically varied surface roughness (Ra = 10 nm, 50 nm, 100 nm) at 900 K and 1200 K
Measure the standard deviation of the friction coefficient over the sliding cycle for each roughness level
evidence_spans: Also, we did not study the roughness of the material surface.

With the increase of temperature, the friction coefficients gradually increased, and the fluctuation range also continued to increase. When the temperature rose from 900 K to 1200 K, there was a large increase, and the fluctuation was more intense.
This might be due to a large number of surface defects in the Cu matrix under the high temperature environment, which hindered the generation of line defect dislocation.
